# Synthesis: The Capstone Debates {#sec-debates}

## Required route and purpose

Read this chapter and the short common brief for the debate you are preparing. No full paper or optional technical extension becomes required because it appears in a bibliography. The four debates occur April 20, April 22, April 27 and April 29, 2027.

The course began with a user making a decision. Certainty linked cash flows to value; uncertainty and private information made that link harder. Accrual accounting addressed timing and measurement. Market evidence asked what reported numbers reveal. Internal accounting showed that reports also change choices. The debates bring those functions together.

For each claim, distinguish a model prediction, an observed association, a constructed example and a causal conclusion. The absence of a cash payment does not mean the absence of an economic cost. A numerical estimate does not remove uncertainty. A disclosure can both reveal information and change incentives.

## An argument readers can evaluate

Name a user and decision. Explain the proposed mechanism using the course framework. Supply evidence appropriate to that claim, acknowledge an alternative explanation, and identify an observation that would change your conclusion. A precise conditional argument is better than a sweeping assertion supported by an unrelated paper.

Both teams must address the strongest objection to their assigned position. Random assignment is a way to practice that discipline, not a request to adopt the position personally. Cite the actual source and the assigned passage; an AI-generated citation is not evidence.

## Debate 1: mandatory climate-related disclosure

**April 20. Resolved: A mandatory, standardized climate-related financial disclosure regime would improve capital allocation enough to justify its compliance costs.**

Consider economically material risks to the reporting organization, usable measurement, enforcement and burdens on firms of different sizes. The affirmative should explain how information changes a decision. The negative should compare the proposed regime with a feasible alternative, including costs of missing or inconsistent information.

This is a policy comparison, not a claim that a particular current rule has already produced measured benefits. The SEC adopted climate-disclosure rules in 2024, stayed them during litigation and proposed rescinding them in May 2026. A proposal to rescind is not a completed rescission. The dated institutional note must be rechecked before the debate. [SEC May 29, 2026 fact sheet](https://www.sec.gov/files/33-11421-fact-sheet.pdf).

The common brief supplies a **constructed** benefit/cost comparison. It cannot establish the effect of an actual rule. IFRS-adoption findings or stock-price associations are not direct experiments on the proposed climate policy.

## Debate 2: goodwill measurement

**April 22. Resolved: For a public company, acquired goodwill should be remeasured annually with both upward and downward changes recognized in income, instead of the current impairment model.**

For this hypothetical proposal, remeasure only the acquired-goodwill component using an explicitly documented allocation of reporting-unit value; do not recognize new internally generated goodwill separately. This restriction does not solve the difficult problem of separating the acquired component from subsequently created value. Teams must address it.

The required baseline is the public-company impairment model discussed in Chapter 8: goodwill is not routinely amortized, and impairment assessment occurs annually and between annual tests when qualifying circumstances arise. Eligible private-company/not-for-profit alternatives are outside this resolution. Annual impairment testing is not the same as unrestricted annual upward/downward remeasurement. [FASB ASU 2017-04](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU2017-04.pdf).

Compare delayed recognition with estimation uncertainty, managerial discretion, verification cost and implications for contracts. Do not promise that a fair-value estimate removes discretion or that an impairment-only carrying amount is an observable current value.

## Debate 3: share-based compensation and performance measures

**April 27. Resolved: A board should exclude expense for equity-classified employee service awards from its primary annual operating-performance measure.**

Use the simple service awards from Chapter 10: grant-date value is supplied, service is recognized over the specified period, and no forfeiture, modification, tax or diluted-EPS complication is required. The proposal changes the board's internal primary performance measure, not GAAP recognition.

Both sides must acknowledge that employee services have a cost even when payment is in shares. The affirmative can argue that a particular annual measure should separate compensation policy from operating execution, but must explain how the board will still hold decision-makers accountable for the cost. The negative can argue that exclusion rewards substitution toward stock pay or obscures resource use, but must consider whether supplementary measures address a real comparison problem. Assess a reconciled GAAP-to-adjusted measure and the incentives it creates.

This replaces the earlier tax-deductibility resolution. No tax-law or option-pricing prerequisite is added.

## Debate 4: hidden characteristics and hidden actions

**April 29. Resolved: The principal benefit of mandatory sustainability reporting is improved accountability for hidden actions, rather than better information about hidden characteristics.**

Moral hazard is a form of information asymmetry. The distinction here is **hidden action versus hidden characteristics**, not moral hazard versus information. A report can affect both. Specify a setting, a stakeholder and an outcome before arguing which mechanism is primary.

For example, emissions information might help a lender distinguish otherwise similar borrowers and might also help a board evaluate a manager's subsequent choices. External harm is not automatically hidden action: an observable externality can still motivate policy. Reporting alone may not change behavior unless users can act on what is learned.

## Classroom format and preparation

The instructor randomly assigns **eight speaking teams**, two per debate, separately from project groups. Each student belongs to one speaking team and contributes to its argument; other students serve as the audience on that date. Three audience members provide advisory evaluations. Publish the team roster and positions by March 30 so preparation time is equal.

Each team sends its constructive argument to the instructor and opponent **48 hours before its debate**, as the syllabus requires. At a 9:05 a.m. class time, deadlines are April 18, April 20, April 25 and April 27 at 9:05 a.m. Eastern. Begin with independent reasoning; follow the syllabus's debate-specific AI rules. There is no additional late-unit individual essay.

The first three meetings use a 60-minute debate: two 8-minute constructives, two 4-minute cross-examinations, two 5-minute rebuttals, two 3-minute conclusions, and 20 minutes of audience questions. Add a 5-minute opening, 7-minute evidence debrief and 3-minute exit note for a 75-minute meeting.

The final debate uses 45 minutes: two 6-minute constructives, two 3-minute cross-examinations, two 4-minute rebuttals, two 2-minute conclusions, and 15 minutes of audience questions. Add a 5-minute opening, 5-minute evidence debrief and 20-minute retrospective.

## Evaluation rubric

The debate category remains **15% of the course**. The instructor assigns the grade using this rubric; peer evaluations inform feedback. Winning the audience vote does not determine the grade.

| Component | Points | Evidence of successful work |
|---|---:|---|
| Constructive argument | 25 | Defined decision, coherent mechanism, relevant evidence |
| Cross-examination | 15 | Specific questions testing assumptions or source interpretation |
| Rebuttal | 25 | Direct, fair response to the strongest objection |
| Use of course framework | 25 | Accurate distinctions and calibrated causal claims |
| Audience questions | 10 | Clear answers, acknowledged limits and useful clarification |
| Total | 100 | |

Within each component, full credit requires accuracy and support; roughly three-quarters indicates a sound argument with a material gap; half indicates partial understanding with weak support; minimal credit reflects unsupported or mistaken claims. The default is a shared team score, with contribution adjustments under the syllabus. Collect members' roles and the source list with the constructive.

## Project feedback and retrospective

Project preliminary findings use a common **one-page gallery exhibit due April 18 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern**, before all final reports. Each team receives one assigned peer response and instructor feedback by April 22. The same opportunity applies to every group, independent of enrollment. Selected exhibits may inform discussion; no group waits until after its final report to receive its first feedback.

The project report is due **before class April 29**. It remains in its own 15% category. The final class's one-page retrospective is participation work: identify one durable insight, one revised belief supported by evidence, one topic that needed more time, and one change you would make to the course. It is not a substitute for the cumulative final.

Optional further reading can deepen any debate. Required assessment uses the chapter's distinctions and supplied briefs rather than technical knowledge from optional originals.
